study_data.study_comment: The study is about examining whether changes in the Simon effect are exclusively driven by the fading of distractor-based activation over time. Using a visual Simon task, the authors manipulated perceptual target discriminability by varying the ratio of red and blue colored dots, thereby creating easy and difficult target discrimination conditions and investigating their effects through delta plot and diffusion model analyses.

dataset_data.group_description: Undergraduates from the University of Hagen
dataset_data.fixation_cross: A black plus sign served as a fixation point. At the beginning of each trial, it appeared on the screen for 500 ms.
dataset_data.data_excl: For both RT and error rate analyses, they excluded trials with RTs < 200ms as anticipations (0.03%) and trials without any response (0.34%). For RT analyses, they additionally excluded choice errors (3.87%). Four participants were excluded because of error rates of 20% or higher. The final dataset then consisted of 115 participants. The first two blocks were considered practice and not analyzed.

within_condition_details.name: The proportion of colored dots was 37.5% versus 62.5% (hard condition, low perceptual target discriminability). Perceptual target discriminability varied randomly within blocks.
The proportion of colored dots was 10% versus 90% (easy condition, high perceptual target discriminability). Perceptual target discriminability varied randomly within blocks.

dataset_data.group_description: Undergraduates from the University of Hagen
dataset_data.fixation_cross: A black plus sign served as a fixation point. At the beginning of each trial, it appeared on the screen for 500 ms.
dataset_data.data_excl: For both RT and error rate analyses, they excluded trials with RTs < 200ms as anticipations (0.15%) and trials without any response (0.34%). For RT analyses, they additionally excluded choice errors (4.51%). Two participants were excluded because of error rates of 20% or higher.  The final dataset then consisted of 121 participants. within_condition_details.name: The proportion of colored dots was 37.5% versus 62.5% (hard condition, low perceptual target discriminability). Target discriminability was kept constant within a block and alternated between blocks. Half of the participants began with a high discriminability block, while the other half started with a low discriminability block.

The proportion of colored dots was 10% versus 90% (easy condition, high perceptual target discriminability). Target discriminability was kept constant within a block and alternated between blocks. Half of the participants began with a high discriminability block, while the other half started with a low discriminability block.

publication_data.title: Perceptual Target Discriminability Modulates the Simon Effect Beyond the Fading of Distractor-Based Activation: Insights From Delta Plots and Diffusion Model Analyses
publication_data.apa_reference: Ellinghaus, R., Liepelt, R., Mackenzie, I. G., & Mittelstädt, V. (2024). Perceptual target discriminability modulates the Simon effect beyond the fading of distractor-based activation: Insights from delta plots and diffusion model analyses. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 50(8), 842–858. https://doi.org/10.1037/ xhp0001211
publication_data.keywords: conflict tasks, selective attention, diffusion model, Simon task, delta plots

task_data.task_description: In the visual Simon task, participants are instructed to respond with key presses to a specific feature (color) of a target presented to the left or right of the center. In the present study, target stimuli were squares consisting of multiple blue and red dots which appeared to the left or right side from the center of the screen. Participants had to determine whether there were primarily red or blue dots by pressing a left or right key. Responses were key presses with the left and right index finger on the “Q” and “P” keys of a computer keyboard.
